name: Digital Twins for Experiments
title: Digital Twins for Experiments
answer: Digital twins for experiments are software replicas of a physical experimental setup, kept in step with the real instrument through a stream of measurements. In a laboratory they cover a single rig, such as a bioreactor or a flow cell, or a whole bench with several instruments and a robot arm. The twin is used to plan runs, watch a run as it happens, and test changes that would be slow, costly or unsafe to try on the real apparatus. It sits between laboratory automation, which moves and measures things, and simulation, which predicts what the apparatus will do.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Digital twins for experiments are software replicas of a physical experimental setup, kept in step with the real instrument through a stream of measurements. In a laboratory they cover a single rig, such as a bioreactor or a flow cell, or a whole bench with several instruments and a robot arm. The twin is used to plan runs, watch a run as it happens, and test changes that would be slow, costly or unsafe to try on the real apparatus. It sits between laboratory automation, which moves and measures things, and simulation, which predicts what the apparatus will do.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A twin runs on a model of the apparatus, a data pipeline from the instruments, and a store that keeps the run history. The model may be a physics simulation, a machine learning surrogate trained on earlier runs, or a mix of the two, and it is refreshed as new measurements arrive. Instrument links use common laboratory protocols and file formats, with a scheduler or workflow engine to start runs and a database or data lake to hold results. Compute ranges from a workstation beside the bench to a cluster when the simulation is heavy.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work starts by capturing the geometry, settings and behaviour of the real apparatus, then fitting or calibrating a model until its predictions match recorded runs. During an experiment the twin ingests live readings, updates its state, and can flag drift between predicted and observed values. Researchers then run candidate conditions inside the twin before committing them to the bench, and the results of the real run are fed back to improve the model. This loop of calibrate, predict, run and correct is what keeps the twin useful rather than decorative.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: A twin inherits the rights and risks of the experiment it mirrors, including ownership of the underlying data, consent and ethics approvals where samples come from people, and biosafety or chemical rules for the physical rig. Provenance matters because a prediction is only as good as the model version, calibration data and instrument settings behind it, so runs should be traceable to the original records. Access control separates those who can change the model from those who can only read it, and audit logs record who altered settings and when. Where a twin informs a regulated submission, the model itself may need documented validation.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward twins that stay live across many runs, share a common description of laboratory equipment, and connect to one another so a change on one bench is visible on another. Better surrogate models and cheaper compute make it practical to keep a twin running alongside the experiment rather than only before it. Standards for describing instruments and for exchanging run data are still forming, and that gap is the main obstacle to twins moving between laboratories. Expect more emphasis on proving that a twin still matches its physical counterpart as apparatus ages and is modified.
